tldr: We introduce EgoGenEval, a benchmark designed to evaluate whether visual generators follow language-guided camera motion while physically and consistently preserving the 3D scene state. Evaluating 16 recent models revealed that no system successfully grounds camera motion while preserving the scene, and standard pairwise supervised fine-tuning fails to overcome this barrier.
hero_caption: Overview of EgoGenEval. Across Atomic (single-step), Chain (3-step sequential), and Cycle (round-trip) protocols, it strictly separates and measures Camera Motion Grounding (CMG) and Scene State Preservation (SSP) at the geometric and object levels. As the top-right results show, no current model achieves high scores on both axes simultaneously.
overview:
Recent advances in image generation models and world models allow them to produce photorealistic images. This has spurred momentum toward using them as visual simulators for spatial reasoning and embodied planning in robotics. However, when a robot issues a command like "move forward 0.3m," does the generator actually move the camera by that specified distance without collapsing the furniture and room layout? Existing benchmarks largely focus on isolated image aesthetics or settings where explicit camera poses are provided, leaving the physical consistency of models driven purely by natural language instructions underexplored.

To address this, the authors built EgoGenEval, a geometry-grounded benchmark. The evaluation is clearly decoupled into two axes: whether the model executed the commanded camera motion (CMG score) and whether the state of the environment that should be visible from the target viewpoint is preserved (SSP score). Furthermore, in addition to single-step motions, realistic robot control protocols were designed: 3-step continuous motions (Chain), "there and back" round trips (Cycle), and varying amounts of reference context images ($K=1\sim 4$).

Evaluating 16 state-of-the-art generators revealed striking shortcomings. While models can roughly predict the direction of camera motion, they fail to accurately ground its scale. Moreover, even when the camera reaches the correct position, objects in the room frequently vanish or distort. In multi-step settings where self-generated images are fed into the next step, state degradation accelerates rapidly. Furthermore, controlled fine-tuning experiments using EgoGen-Train—a large-scale dataset built with the exact same pipeline—showed that single-step pairwise supervision improves motion grounding while barely helping scene preservation, exposing a fundamental limitation of the standard training objective itself.
contributions: Introducing EgoGenEval, a geometry-grounded, language-driven benchmark containing 1,400 cases and 2,360 target views that separately measures Camera Motion Grounding (CMG) and Scene State Preservation (SSP)
Establishing evaluation protocols mimicking embodied robot rollouts, including single-step motions, 3-step sequences, round trips, and variable surrounding visual contexts
Demonstrating across 16 pose-free generators that visual quality dissociates from physical consistency, exposing a deep trade-off between motion execution and scene preservation
Conducting SFT experiments on the large-scale EgoGen-Train dataset, pinpointing an inherent bottleneck in traditional single-step pairwise supervision for improving scene preservation

sections.heading: Visual fidelity does not guarantee physical correctness
sections.summary: To serve as simulators for robotics, visual generators must accurately execute commanded camera motions while preserving the physical state of the scene. However, existing benchmarks conflate these two abilities, failing to properly assess them. This work addresses this gap with EgoGenEval, decoupling motion execution from scene preservation.
sections.details:
Recent visual generators produce remarkably realistic images. Consequently, expectations are high for using them as simulators for visual imagination and spatial reasoning in robotics. Yet, to function as a simulator, an instruction like "move 30 cm to the left" requires the model to execute that exact motion while preserving the identity, appearance, and layout of objects in the room. In practice, even if generated images look plausible at a glance, models frequently fail to move from the source viewpoint, overshoot drastically, or drop pieces of furniture into thin air.

Prior benchmarks have focused predominantly on text-to-image synthesis quality, single-image editing, or setups where a rigid 6-DoF camera pose matrix is provided from the outset. There was no unified testbed to evaluate whether models driven solely by natural language camera instructions can maintain physical consistency across multiple steps, as an embodied robot must.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed EgoGenEval, curating 1,400 cases (2,360 target views) from real-world indoor RGB-D scans. The evaluation is structured along two axes: Camera Motion Grounding (CMG), which captures instruction following in camera motion, and Scene State Preservation (SSP), which tracks whether object layouts and appearances remain intact. Both metrics correlate strongly with blinded human judgments. Across 16 evaluated models, not a single one excelled on both axes at once, revealing that perceptual quality often disguises physical failure.

sections.heading: Where existing benchmarks fall short: bridging language control and 3D consistency
sections.summary: While image generation evaluation, novel view synthesis, and world model benchmarks have each targeted key aspects, a unified framework evaluating language-guided camera control and strict 3D scene preservation in a rollout format was missing. EgoGenEval bridges these domains.
sections.details:
### Image Generation and Geometric Consistency Benchmarks
Prior evaluations in image generation focused heavily on whether specified objects are correctly depicted (syntactic compliance) or on localized single-image editing precision. For video generation, some benchmarks evaluate epipolar geometric residuals (e.g., PDI-Bench), but they do not directly diagnose whether a generator precisely follows a specified camera displacement.

### Novel View Synthesis and Camera-Controlled Generation
In novel view synthesis (NVS) like NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting, as well as some world model benchmarks, perfectly calibrated camera poses (pose matrices) are provided as inputs. In human and generalist agent interactions, however, pose-free generators that operate on linguistic instructions like "turn slightly to the right" are required. EgoGenEval sets itself apart by focusing on systems driven solely by language without explicit pose matrices.

### World Models and Embodied Evaluation
Evaluations of action-conditioned world models increasingly assess task success rates and interaction dynamics in simulators. However, current generators cannot even satisfy the most foundational requirement of static geometric consistency: does a static room remain intact with correct parallax when the observer moves? EgoGenEval zeroes in on this essential foundation.

sections.heading: Deterministically generating rigorous geometric test cases from real-world 3D scans
sections.summary: Using real-world RGB-D data from sources like ScanNet++, the benchmark constructs tasks covering four canonical motions, 3-step continuous chains, and round trips. Deterministic numerical language prompts are generated from camera poses, and the number of reference context views is carefully controlled.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Tasks, Context, and Motion Taxonomy
The inputs are a current view image $I_s$, a natural language instruction $T$ containing direction and explicit magnitude (e.g., "move forward by approximately 0.3m"), and optional auxiliary context views $C$ of the same scene. The model generates the target view $\hat{I}_t$ after motion. To mimic a robot utilizing past visual memory, the total number of input images $K$ varies from 1 (source only) to 2, 3, and 4 (up to 3 context images).

Motions are categorized into four canonical robot primitives: forward/backward ($z$), left/right lateral translation ($x$), yaw rotation (horizontal panning), and pitch rotation (vertical tilting). Three protocols are established: single-step (Atomic), autoregressive 3-step sequences (Chain), and "there-and-back" round trips of equal magnitude (Cycle).

### 3.2 Benchmark Construction Pipeline
The construction pipeline proceeds in three phases (Figure F2(a)):
- **Phase 1 (Geometric Transition Mining)**: From ScanNet++, ScanNet, Hypersim, and Matterport3D, frame pairs satisfying overlap and co-visibility criteria where the primary motion component dominates all others are mined.
- **Phase 2 (Task Assembly and Language Generation)**: Using ground-truth relative poses and deterministic templates, instructions embedding precise directions and metric/degree magnitudes are automatically generated. Context views are prioritized and chosen via geometric scoring to provide reconstructive cues without revealing the target view itself.
- **Phase 3 (Quality Filtering and Balanced Sampling)**: Following z-buffer occlusion checks, VLM-based visual and anchor checks, and human verification, 1,400 cases (2,360 target views) across 771 scenes were finalized. Cases are balanced across subtypes and $K$ splits (50:35:10:5).

captions.F2: EgoGenEval construction pipeline (a) and dataset composition (b). Through rigorous geometric filtering, VLM quality control, and human validation, 1,400 cases spanning four canonical motions, three chain sequences, and two cycle variants are assembled, balanced across context view counts K.

sections.heading: Decoupling motion execution from scene preservation with two dedicated metrics
sections.summary: The framework defines the CMG score to measure motion direction and magnitude via a relative pose estimator, and the SSP score to grade scene preservation via object detection, depth ordering, and appearance matching. Both metrics correlate strongly with blinded human judgments.
sections.details:
To evaluate physical consistency, the benchmark strictly decouples camera motion fidelity from scene state preservation.

### 4.1 Evaluation Setup
The benchmark evaluates 16 recent pose-free generators driven purely by language instructions (open-weight and proprietary image editing models, multimodal models, and video generators). Two pose-conditioned reference world models that accept exact 6-DoF trajectories are also evaluated. For Chain and Cycle protocols, models perform autoregressive rollouts where each generated frame serves as the input to the subsequent step.

### 4.2 CMG (Camera Motion Grounding): Did it move as instructed?
A pre-trained relative pose estimator (DA3Nested-Giant-Large) predicts motion parameters between the source and generated views. Translation scale is calibrated against ground-truth geometry using a global factor $\alpha_m$ shared across all models. The step score $g_m = d_m \times (0.5 + 0.5 q_m)$ combines directional sign agreement ($d_m \in \{0, 1\}$) and magnitude fidelity ($q_m \in [0, 1]$) via a sigmoid relative-error function. Reversing or missing the direction results in an immediate zero score.

### 4.3 SSP (Scene State Preservation): Is the environment preserved?
How well objects that should appear in the target view are preserved is evaluated across three pillars:
1. **Object Recall ($F_1$)**: Grounding DINO and a VLM object matcher establish one-to-one correspondences between ground-truth and generated objects.
2. **Spatial Topology ($\mathcal{S}$)**: Evaluates pairwise 2D planar direction agreement ($O^{xy}$), relative depth ordering ($O^z$), and normalized centroid error among objects.
3. **Appearance Integrity ($\mathcal{I}$)**: Computes a weighted combination of DINO feature discriminability, SSIM, edge similarity, sharpness, color, and aspect-ratio preservation for matched objects.
These pillars are averaged, incorporating a bottleneck penalty across multi-step sequences to yield the final SSP score (Figure F8).

### 4.4 Aggregation and Alignment with Human Judgment
The Overall score is the unweighted mean of CMG and SSP. Validation against blinded human evaluations (340 steps, three annotators) yielded high system-level rank correlations (Spearman $\rho = 0.943$, Kendall $\tau_b = 0.867$). Furthermore, swapping the pose or depth estimator backends left the system rankings virtually unchanged, confirming metric robustness.

captions.F8: Step-by-step calculation of the SSP score. Objects are detected in both ground-truth and generated views, matched one-to-one, and evaluated across relative 2D positions, pairwise depth ordering, and multi-faceted appearance similarity.

sections.heading: Experimental findings: moving melts the scene, keeping the scene freezes the camera
sections.summary: Evaluating 16 models uncovered a trade-off between CMG and SSP, severe magnitude undershooting, compounding roll-out collapses, and context view hallucination. Furthermore, fine-tuning on 100k pairs yielded minimal scene preservation gains, exposing the ceiling of pairwise supervision.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Main Evaluation Findings
The top-ranking model, GPT-Image-2, achieved an Overall score of 0.662, remaining far below the ground-truth oracle (0.940). Key findings include:

- **Motion-Scene Trade-off**: Models with high CMG show low SSP, and vice versa. HY-WorldMirror achieved the highest CMG (0.847) but struggled on SSP (0.481). Conversely, FLUX.2-dev reached a high SSP of 0.554 while yielding a low CMG of 0.448. In short, systems either move the camera at the cost of melting the world, or preserve the world by staying put.
- **Correct Direction, Wrong Magnitude**: Directional accuracy was relatively high at 66.3%, driving model CMG rankings ($\rho = 0.997$). However, among directionally correct cases, 60–70% deviated from the requested displacement by more than $\pm 20\%$. Undershooting worsened significantly for larger target displacements.
- **Compounding Autoregressive Collapse**: Moving from single-step (Atomic) to 3-step sequences (Chain), SSP dropped by an average of 0.164 across all 16 models (Figure F4(b)). In Cycle tests, while 37.4% of cases remained stationary on the forward step, 66.3% stayed nearly stationary (motion ratio $\le 0.2$) on the return step after conditioning on self-generated frames.
- **Context Views are Copied, Not Synthesized**: Increasing context views $K$ from 1 to 4 improved CMG (0.519 $\to$ 0.582) but degraded SSP (0.539 $\to$ 0.504). In 62.2% of multi-view generations, the output matched an auxiliary view more closely than the target, revealing that models copy context images directly rather than fusing them into novel viewpoints.
- **Visual Quality Dissociates from Physical Consistency**: Perceptual visual quality (VisQual) had virtually no correlation with SSP ($\rho = 0.292$). For example, Step1X-Edit ranked first in visual similarity metrics but was the worst pose-free model on CMG (0.298). Despite looking realistic, it barely moved.

### 5.2 Large-Scale Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
Using EgoGen-Train (66,214 trajectories, 108,213 pairs) constructed from held-out scenes, models like Qwen-Image-Edit were fine-tuned with LoRA.
Qwen's Overall score improved from 0.495 to 0.681. However, this gain was heavily asymmetric: CMG surged by $+0.303$, while SSP gained only $+0.069$. Scaling the training data to full capacity, tripling the training budget, or evaluating single-step cases without compounding errors still left SSP gains at a fraction of CMG improvements. On another architecture, OmniGen2, fine-tuning failed to improve CMG and actually degraded SSP.

This asymmetry proves that the bottleneck is not data scarcity, but the pairwise teacher-forced training objective itself. Next-frame prediction losses encourage matching camera transitions, but offer little incentive to maintain 3D object persistence and spatial geometry.

captions.F4: Representative failure modes. (a) Under single-step right yaw rotation, models exhibit rotation undershooting, furniture disappearance, visual artifacts, reversed rotation, and stationary copying. (b) Across a 3-step chain, room contents progressively dissolve despite strong motion grounding (CMG). (c) In round-trip cycles, a model executes the forward step but moves in the wrong direction on the return step.

sections.heading: The persistent state bottleneck and implications for future research
sections.summary: Visual generators emulate camera transitions without maintaining a persistent underlying 3D state. Limitations of this benchmark include its focus on static indoor environments and rollouts capped at three steps.
sections.details:
### The Persistent State Bottleneck
This study highlights a fundamental issue: current visual generators are adept at creating images that resemble camera motion, but fail to maintain an internal, persistent 3D scene state upon which actions operate. Models follow directional signs but cannot ground metric scales, hallucinate by copying context views, and fail to execute inverse motions when conditioned on their own outputs.

As the SFT experiments showed, simply training on clean pairwise frames cannot resolve this issue. For visual generators to serve as reliable simulators for robotics, a paradigm shift is needed: models must undergo trajectory-level training with self-conditioned rollouts, coupled with explicit geometric supervision such as 3D bounding boxes, depth, and visibility constraints.

### Limitations
- **Scope of Environments and Motion**: The benchmark is restricted to static indoor scenes, four canonical camera primitives, and short rollouts of up to three steps. Dynamic objects, long-horizon navigation, and complex physical manipulation interactions remain unexplored.
- **Evaluator Dependency**: Because CMG and SSP rely on pre-trained perceptual models (pose estimators and object detectors), perceptual misclassifications could influence scores. However, high correlation with blinded human judgments and extensive ablations confirm that overall system rankings remain dependable.

sections.heading: Conclusion: new directions in evaluation and training for embodied intelligence
sections.summary: Through EgoGenEval, an extensive evaluation of 16 models, and SFT experiments, this work exposed the deep divide between camera motion grounding and scene state preservation. Maintaining a persistent static world remains an open challenge, necessitating a shift toward trajectory-centric training.
sections.details:
This paper presented EgoGenEval, a geometry-grounded benchmark designed to rigorously assess the physical consistency of visual generators under language-guided ego-motion. Across 16 pose-free models, separating motion execution from scene preservation uncovered critical trade-offs that aggregate perceptual scores fail to capture.

Furthermore, controlled SFT experiments on EgoGen-Train demonstrated that pairwise teacher-forced supervision faces severe limitations in improving scene preservation. To build visual simulators capable of true spatial intelligence and embodied planning, future research must move beyond training on isolated frame pairs toward trajectory-level reinforcement learning, self-conditioned rollouts, and explicit geometric regularizations on pose and visibility. EgoGenEval provides a robust compass to track that progress.

sections.heading: Appendix: qualitative failure gallery and metric robustness
sections.summary: The appendix details failure galleries across atomic, chain, and cycle settings, ablation experiments verifying metric robustness, and the dataset composition of EgoGen-Train.
sections.details:
### Single-Step and Rollout Failure Galleries
Figures F9 and F10 illustrate the failure modes observed across models:
- **Single-Step Failures (Figure F9)**: Models exhibit stationary copies that fail to move under lateral commands (Step1X-Edit), extreme overshooting that phases through walls during forward movement (HY-WorldMirror), wrong-way rotations, and instant disappearance of wall-adjacent furniture upon turning.
- **Rollout Failures (Figure F10)**: In 3-step mixed sequences (C3), the count of preserved objects drops sharply across steps ($2/2 \to 1/7 \to 0/2$), leaving only an empty white wall in the final frame—demonstrating "object memory collapse." In Cycle tests, models that succeed on the forward step often generate blank white frames or move further away when instructed to return.

### Metric Robustness and Dataset Analysis
Replacing the relative pose estimator from DA3 to VGGT-1B retained a CMG rank correlation of $\rho = 0.943$. SSP was similarly stable under alternative depth backends ($\rho = 1.000$) and detection threshold variations ($\rho \ge 0.929$). Furthermore, excluding ScanNet++ (the majority source) and re-evaluating exclusively on other sources produced identical top-tier rankings, proving that the findings do not overfit to a specific data source.

captions.F9: Failure gallery in single-step (Atomic) motions. Rows show forward/backward, lateral translation, yaw, and pitch motions, highlighting distinct model failures such as directional reversal, magnitude over/undershooting, and object vanishing (M/G: matched vs. ground-truth object count).
captions.F10: Rollout failure gallery in Chain and Cycle settings. In 3-step sequences (a, b), objects progressively disappear with each step. In cycle motions (c, d, e), models correctly execute the forward step but reverse direction or hallucinate entirely new scenes on the return step.

takeaways: Visual photorealism in image generators does not guarantee that camera motions are executed correctly or that 3D scene structures are physically preserved.
Current models generally capture motion direction, but their control over motion magnitude is severely broken, heavily undershooting requested distances.
Autoregressive rollouts using self-generated frames trigger rapid scene degradation; evaluating models on isolated single steps obscures this failure.
Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on single-step image pairs only boosts camera motion execution while failing to improve scene preservation, demanding new trajectory-centric training paradigms.
limitations: Restricted to static indoor scenes; dynamic objects, robot-environment physical contacts, and manipulation interactions are not evaluated.
Sequential rollout evaluation is limited to a maximum of three steps, leaving long-horizon memory maintenance in extended navigation unverified.
CMG and SSP rely on pre-trained perceptual backends (such as DA3 and Grounding DINO), leaving room for evaluator perception errors to influence scores.
